content: 1. Roles and Responsibilities in Vaccine Deployment: Members of deployment committees and other key authorities are tasked with preparing duty rosters and planning vaccine shipments, including determining the mode of transport. They oversee critical aspects such as vaccine and ancillary supply forecasting, reception, storage, transportation, distribution, and immunization waste management. Processes and formats are established for data collection, analysis, visualization, and communication using management information systems, inventory management, and health facility capacity assessments. A system for monitoring and evaluating deployment activities is also implemented. 2. Simulation Exercises for Pandemic Preparedness: Countries are encouraged to conduct simulation exercises as part of their pandemic preparedness planning. These exercises help refine and update National Deployment and Vaccination Plans (NDVPs). Resources such as the Pandemic Influenza Preparedness (PIP) Deploy tabletop gaming exercise and COVID-19-specific vaccine tabletop exercises (focusing on regulatory, safety, supply chain, and communication issues) are available to assist countries. It is recommended that all relevant stakeholders, including vaccine manufacturers, participate in these exercises. 3. Key Takeaways for Effective Vaccination Campaigns: Strong political leadership is essential for the successful rollout of vaccination campaigns. Enhanced coordination between national and sub-national levels can fast-track pandemic vaccination efforts, especially by clarifying roles, responsibilities, and focal points. Countries should identify individuals responsible for key activities with clear terms of reference and accountability. 4. Defining and Identifying Key Populations: During pandemics caused by novel viruses, the World Health Organization (WHO) Strategic Advisory Group of Experts (SAGE) provides global guidance on key groups for vaccination. National Immunization Technical Advisory Groups (NITAGs) are expected to adapt SAGE guidance to their national context, considering public health goals and prioritization approaches. While it is impossible to predict specific target populations for future pandemics, advance planning during inter-pandemic periods can expedite the identification of key populations. 5. Criteria for Identifying Key Populations: WHO SAGE developed a values framework and roadmap during the COVID-19 pandemic to guide vaccine allocation and prioritization. This framework emphasizes principles such as human well-being, equity, reciprocity, and legitimacy. Countries can use this framework as a blueprint for future pandemic preparedness planning. 6. Linkages to Public Health Goals: 7. Data Sources for Estimating Key Population Sizes: Routine vaccination data, national statistics, health worker registries, and disease registries can help estimate the size of key populations. Countries should avoid double counting individuals who belong to multiple groups, as seen in past pandemic experiences. 8. National Allocation and Prioritization Considerations: In the event of vaccine shortages during a pandemic, countries must make decisions about vaccine allocation and prioritization based on principles such as equity, reciprocity, and emerging scientific evidence. Strategies should align with public health goals and lessons learned from previous pandemics. 9. Digital Microplanning and Geospatial Data: Investments in digital microplanning can strengthen health systems and improve coordination across programs. 10. Vaccination Delivery Strategies: Countries should adopt a mix of vaccine delivery strategies, such as fixed sites, mobile clinics, and outreach programs, to maximize coverage and reach underserved populations. Comprehensive microplans should account for resource implications, including financial and human resources. 11. IPC is critical during vaccination campaigns, especially in the early phases of a pandemic when vaccine availability is limited. 12. Integration with Other Health Interventions: Over time, pandemic vaccination efforts may be integrated with routine health services to optimize resource utilization. Mechanisms such as antenatal clinics and chronic disease clinics can be used to vaccinate high-risk groups. 13. Community Engagement and Mobilization: Engaging communities through surveys, focus groups, and public meetings can increase vaccine acceptance and uptake. Mobilization efforts should include reminders for registered beneficiaries and follow-ups for those who miss vaccination sessions. 14. Planning for Adverse Events Following Immunization (AEFIs): Vaccination teams should be equipped to manage emergencies such as anaphylaxis and have transport available for referrals to institutional care. 15. Immunization Schedule Planning: WHO will provide recommended immunization schedules for approved pandemic vaccines based on clinical trial findings. Countries should consider vaccine interchangeability, co-administration, and specific needs of vulnerable groups in their schedules. This detailed explanation provides a comprehensive understanding of the strategies, considerations, and best practices for pandemic vaccination planning and implementation.
